slides.title: Ziehl–Neelsen staining
bullets: 1. Place several smears on the rack so that they do not touch; flood each with carbon-fuchsin solution.
2. Light a cotton swab dipped in alcohol and heat the slides evenly; as soon as steam appears set the clock for 5 minutes. Do not let the dye boil or overheat; if it begins to dry, add dye gently.
3. Pour off the dye and wash the smear gently with water until it is colourless; hold the slide tilted.

slides.title: Ziehl–Neelsen staining
bullets: 4. To decolourise, flood with acid alcohol for 3 minutes; wash gently with water.
5. Make sure the smear is completely decolourised; if traces of carbol-fuchsin remain, continue with acid alcohol.
6. Cover the smear with methylene blue for 30 seconds.

slides.title: Sources of error, reading and quality control
bullets: If the dye boils or overheats, or the slide is left dry, the staining is spoiled; leftover water interferes with the next dye.
If the smear is not fully decolourised, traces of carbol-fuchsin spoil the result.
How to read a Ziehl–Neelsen smear (colour, grading and counting) is not given in the source — use the laboratory’s approved instructions.
Internal quality control: keep a set of unstained smears made from positive sputum; check a new batch of dye or another reagent on a control smear stained together with every specimen.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Any sputum may contain tubercle bacilli: work in protective clothing.
Take care with open flame when lighting an alcohol-soaked swab; keep flammable liquids away from fire.
Wear gloves when handling dyes; used slides and solutions are disinfected.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 1/5
bullets: Specimen: Sputum (at least 3 specimens 8–24 hours apart, one early in the morning)

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 2/5
bullets: What it is used for: AFB tests are mainly used to diagnose active TB, especially after a positive TB screening test, an abnormal chest x-ray or symptoms; in people on treatment they show whether it is working and whether the person is still infectious. Symptoms of lung TB include a cough lasting three weeks or more, coughing up blood or sputum, chest pain, fever, night sweats and unexplained weight loss.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 3/5
bullets: Physiology: Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) are bacteria that cause tuberculosis and other mycobacterial infections such as leprosy. There are four tests: smear microscopy (results in 1–2 days but cannot diagnose); culture (confirms the diagnosis, but per MedlinePlus takes 6–8 weeks); a molecular test (NAAT — detects TB bacteria directly in sputum in under two hours and can check rifampicin resistance); and drug susceptibility testing.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 4/5
bullets: Per CDC, an optimal bacteriologic examination has five parts: specimen collection, transport and processing; AFB smear classification; direct detection of M. tuberculosis by nucleic acid amplification (with molecular detection of resistance where applicable); culture and identification; and drug susceptibility testing. Smears are stained and examined for AFB, with results due within 24 hours of collection.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 5/5
bullets: AFB seen are counted and graded 1+, 2+, 3+ or 4+ — the higher the grade, the more infectious the patient.

WHO recommends rapid diagnostic tests — molecular assays and biomarker-based point-of-care tests — as the initial test for everyone with signs and symptoms of TB; they give initial results within 48 hours of sample collection.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result · 1/2
cols: A positive smear means TB or another mycobacterial infection is likely, but culture is needed to confirm: microscopy cannot tell M. tuberculosis from non-tuberculous mycobacteria. Because culture takes weeks, treatment may be started in the meantime. A positive NAAT means TB is probable.

Negative smears do not exclude TB, and a negative culture does not necessarily rule it out — some patients are diagnosed on clinical grounds. A negative result can also mean there were not enough bacteria in the sample.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result · 2/2
cols: Culture is the gold standard for laboratory confirmation: growth of M. tuberculosis confirms TB disease. Drug susceptibility testing is done on the first positive culture; with risk factors for drug resistance or a positive smear or NAA result, specimens go immediately for molecular resistance testing.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: At least three consecutive sputum specimens are examined, collected 8–24 hours apart with at least one early in the morning. Collect them in an airborne infection isolation room, a sputum booth or another isolated, well-ventilated area. Other methods include sputum induction, bronchoscopy and gastric washing.

Sputum is thick mucus coughed up from the lungs, not saliva. Breathe deeply, cough and spit into a sterile container. If not enough comes up, breathing a sterile saline mist can help; if that fails, bronchoscopy is done. Smear and culture are usually done at the same time.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Sputum is usually collected in the morning, and you may be asked to rinse your mouth with water first. The sample is thick sputum coughed up from the lungs, not saliva; the textbooks treat saliva or watery samples as unsuitable.

Limitations: NAA and Xpert MTB/RIF results guide treatment and isolation decisions but do not replace AFB smear, culture, growth-based drug susceptibility testing and genotyping. All specimens should be cultured regardless of the smear result.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: A positive TB blood test (IGRA) or skin test usually means TB infection but does not show active disease — chest x-ray and bacteriology are needed. Some people with TB disease test negative on these. When TB is the presumptive diagnosis, especially in a very ill patient, treatment is not delayed while waiting for bacteriology.
